The workers were angry that Caterpillar had proposed cutting more than 700 jobs and would not negotiate, said Nicolas Benoit, a spokesman for the workers' union. They did not want to harm the Caterpillar executives, Benoit told CNN. One hostage was released Tuesday evening leaving workers with four captives inside the Caterpillar building. The released man was a human resources director identified only as Mr. Petit, because he has heart problems, union representative Bernard Patrick told CNN. About 500 employees were also outside the building protesting. A top Caterpillar executive called the hostage-taking unhelpful. "The actions that are taking place today, led by a small minority of individuals, are not helping as we work for a positive resolution of this situation," said Chris Schena, Caterpillar vice president with responsibility for manufacturing operations in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, in a statement. "The best way to resolve this matter is to continue the negotiations through the Works Council to find a solution that's fair to our employees and allows Caterpillar to remain a leader in a rapidly changing global marketplace," Schena said, adding that the company was "concerned for the safety of our employees." Benoit said all the workers wanted to do was negotiate with Caterpillar and they were upset that the company did not show up to two earlier scheduled negotiating sessions. The employees being held in their office were being allowed to get food, Benoit added. Police arrived at the scene two hours after the incident began but it had not been settled. Employees at a French 3M factory held a manager hostage for more than 24 hours Wednesday and Thursday of last week over a dispute about terms for laid-off staff. Luc Rousselet, who was unharmed, was allowed to leave the plant in Pithiviers, central France, early on Thursday morning after talks between unions and officials from 3M France. **DESPERATE MEASURES: INSIDE FRANCE’S WAVE OF ‘BOSS-NAPPING’**

**GRENOBLE, France** — Inside the executive suite of the Caterpillar tractor factory at the foot of the French Alps, four top managers sat trapped in a glass-walled conference room. Outside, hundreds of angry workers blew whistles, beat on metallic drums, and paced the corridors.

The scene in Grenoble was not a paramilitary hostage crisis, but a distinctly French form of industrial relations known as *"boss-napping"* (or *séquestration*).

The 2009 incident at Caterpillar marked the dramatic peak of a phenomenon that swept France during the global financial crisis. Facing mass layoffs directed by far-off headquarters in North America or Asia, French union workers turned to a radical, illegal, yet strangely polite tactic: locking their bosses in offices until executive management agreed to renegotiate severance deals or save jobs.

### The Caterpillar Siege

The crisis in Grenoble erupted after American heavy-equipment giant Caterpillar announced plans to slash 733 jobs—more than a quarter of the workforce—at its two plants in the Isère region, despite making record profits globally the previous year.

On March 31, 2009, talks between staff and local management collapsed. Refusing to accept the cuts, dozens of workers barricaded the administration building using forklifts and heavy pallets. Trapped inside were four senior executives, including plant director Nicolas Polutnik and human resources chief Jean-Paul Delbos.

For 24 hours, the executives were held captive. Yet, in typical French fashion, the hostage-taking carried a surreal atmosphere of order and hospitality. Workers served the managers coffee, croissants, and sandwiches, and allowed Polutnik to communicate with the press via cell phone.

"We are not criminals, and we have no intention of using physical violence," said Pierre Piccarreta, a senior representative for the CGT (General Confederation of Labour) union at the plant, speaking to reporters through the factory gates during the standoff. "But management needs to understand the violence they are inflicting on us. Taking away a man's livelihood is a form of violence. Holding them in an office for a night is the only language corporate leaders seem to understand when profits come before human lives."

The siege ended only after Caterpillar executives signed a document agreeing to restart talks with mediation from the French government, leading to significantly higher severance packages for those losing their jobs.

Management and business leaders condemned the act as a dangerous breakdown of the rule of law. 

"This is not negotiation; it is illegal coercion," said Laurence Parisot, then-head of the MEDEF, France’s main employers' federation, in a statement reacting to the Caterpillar crisis. "You cannot build a constructive social dialogue when human beings are being held against their will. It damages the reputation of France and sends a terrifying signal to foreign investors."

Polutnik, speaking briefly after his release, described the experience as deeply distressing: "It was an unacceptable pressure tactic. Demands cannot be made at the point of a psychological gun."

### A Contagion of Hostage Negotiations: Sony and 3M

The Caterpillar standoff was not an isolated outburst, but part of a wave of similar actions that caught international corporations off guard.

Just weeks earlier, in March 2009, workers at a **Sony** magnetic tape plant in Pontonx-sur-l’Adour, in southwestern France, locked Chief Executive Serge Foucher in his office overnight. The plant was slated for closure, and workers were furious over what they viewed as paltry severance offers. To block police intervention, workers dumped piles of tree trunks across the factory entrance. Foucher was released 18 hours later after agreeing to reopen severance negotiations—ultimately yielding better terms for the staff.

Days later, at a **3M** pharmaceutical factory in Pithiviers, south of Paris, workers trapped plant director Luc Rousselet in his office for over 24 hours. They demanded better redundancy packages following the announcement of 110 job cuts. Rousselet was famously photographed sitting at his desk, surrounded by workers, eating a meal brought to him by the very employees holding him captive.

"I am a prisoner, but I am being treated correctly," Rousselet told French radio from inside his locked office during the event.

### The Sociology of French Industrial Action

To foreign observers, "boss-napping" appeared to be a lawless insurrection. Yet in France, public sympathy surprisingly swung toward the workers. Polls conducted by the CSA institute at the height of the 2009 wave showed that over 63% of the French public found the boss-nappings "acceptable" or "understandable" given the brutal economic climate.

The phenomenon exploited a specific vacuum in French law enforcement and politics. Under President Nicolas Sarkozy, the French government officially condemned the hostage-takings as illegal. However, authorities rarely dispatched the *Compagnies Républicaines de Sécurité* (CRS) riot police to storm the factories. Politicians feared that violent police crackdowns against workers fighting for their livelihoods would ignite wider civil unrest—a ghost that has haunted French governance since May 1968.

Sociologists noted that boss-napping emerged as a weapon of last resort for a workforce facing the impersonal forces of globalization. When decisions were made in boardrooms in Peoria or Tokyo, local French managers were seen as the only tangible leverage point available to workers.

While the wave of high-profile boss-nappings eventually subsided as the acute shocks of the Great Recession faded, the 2009 events at Caterpillar, Sony, and 3M left an indelible mark on French labor history. They served as a stark reminder to multinational corporations that in France, the social contract is enforced not just in courtrooms, but on the factory floor.

Behind me, you can see a heavy presence of the *CRS*—France’s elite riot police—who have set up a strict security perimeter around the perimeter of the facility. For now, law enforcement appears to be taking a stand-off approach, attempting to negotiate a peaceful resolution through union leaders rather than storming the building. 

Company representatives in the U.S. have issued a brief statement saying they are 'deeply concerned' for the safety of their personnel and are working closely with French authorities. 

We are standing by for a potential press briefing from local officials. As soon as we learn more about the condition of the remaining three executives or the state of negotiations, we will bring it right back to you. 

Wolf, back to you in New York."

# French workers hold Caterpillar executives hostage in job cuts dispute

**GRENOBLE, France (CNN) —** Angry French workers at a Caterpillar manufacturing plant held four top executives, including the head of the company's French operations, hostage inside their offices overnight to demand better severance packages amid sweeping job cuts, company and union officials said Tuesday.

The managers, including Luc Williame, CEO of Caterpillar France, were trapped inside a conference room at the plant in Grenoble, near the French Alps, after negotiations over 733 planned layoffs broke down.

"We are keeping them locked in until we get real negotiations back on the table," Nicolas Benoit, a representative for the CGT labor union, told CNN. "They are being treated humanely. They have food, water, and telephone access, but they are not leaving until management listens to us."

Union members barricaded the doors of the executive suite with tables and metal bars. Outside, hundreds of workers gathered in the courtyard, chanting slogans and burning tires to maintain pressure on the corporate leadership.

### 'Boss-napping' on the rise in France

The incident is the latest in a growing wave of "boss-nappings" across France, as worker anger escalates over job losses triggered by the global economic crisis. 

Just weeks earlier, employees at a Sony plant in southwestern France held the company's French chief executive overnight in a similar dispute. A manager at a 3M facility in France was also recently detained by staff for over 24 hours before agreeing to renegotiate severance packages.

French police were deployed outside the Caterpillar plant to monitor the situation, but authorities have historically avoided intervening violently in such industrial disputes, fearing a wider political backlash or escalation.

Caterpillar, the world's largest manufacturer of construction and mining equipment, announced earlier this year that it would cut up to 20,000 jobs worldwide due to a slump in global demand. The Grenoble plant, which employs roughly 2,700 people, produces tractors and wheeled loaders.

### Management demands release for talks

Corporate spokespeople for Caterpillar Inc., headquartered in Peoria, Illinois, condemned the detention of their executives.

"Holding people against their will is unacceptable and does not create an environment conducive to constructive dialogue," Caterpillar spokesperson Anne-Marie Walsh said in a statement. "We call for the immediate and safe release of our employees so that proper discussions can resume."

Negotiators for the union said they are seeking lower job cuts and significantly higher compensation payouts for those who are let go, arguing that the American parent company has sufficient capital to support its European workforce.

As night fell in Grenoble, union leaders indicated that the executives would remain locked inside the facility until French government mediators or top corporate officials agreed to restart formal talks.
